title: Proboscideans Through Deep Time
intro: Move across deep time to explore how proboscideans changed, dispersed, and declined—and how surviving elephant populations came under increasing human pressure.

eras.label: Paleogene
eras.description: The Paleogene marks the early rise and diversification of proboscideans after the extinction of non-avian dinosaurs. Many foundational mammalian lineages took shape during these intervals.

eras.label: Neogene
eras.description: During the Neogene, proboscideans dispersed widely and diversified across multiple continents. Shifting climates, grassland expansion, and migration patterns made geography central to their evolutionary history.

eras.label: Quaternary
eras.description: The Quaternary includes the great diversity of mammoths, mastodons, and elephantids, as well as the late survival and extinction of many proboscidean groups. It is the key interval for linking paleoecology to human presence.

eras.label: Historical
eras.description: The historical portion of the timeline shifts from deep-time evolution to human systems: trade, empire, extraction, transport, and environmental pressure on living elephant populations.

states.label: Early Proboscideans
states.summary: Early proboscideans emerged in Africa and began diversifying into a range of forms adapted to different environments.
states.interpretation: This state emphasizes origin and diversification. Visitors should distinguish the broader proboscidean order from the much later appearance of modern elephants.
states.question: Why is it misleading to ask when 'elephants' first appeared without distinguishing modern elephants from earlier proboscideans?

states.label: Miocene Dispersal
states.summary: Proboscideans expanded beyond Africa and diversified across Eurasia and other regions.
states.interpretation: Movement across continents makes geography part of evolutionary history. Range maps should be treated as reconstructions based on fossil localities, not perfectly known boundaries.
states.question: What kinds of evidence would allow researchers to reconstruct the geographic spread of proboscideans during the Miocene?

states.label: Pleistocene Diversity
states.summary: Mammoths, mastodons, and other proboscideans occupied wide regions alongside the ancestors and relatives of modern elephants.
states.interpretation: The late Pleistocene shows that recent proboscidean diversity was once much greater than the three living elephant species suggest.
states.question: What does Pleistocene diversity suggest about using the modern distribution of elephants to imagine the past?

states.label: Late Proboscidean Extinctions
states.summary: Many proboscidean lineages disappeared as climate changed and human hunting pressure increased.
states.interpretation: Extinction should not be presented as monocausal. Climate, habitat change, human pressure, and regional variation must be weighed against one another.
states.question: How would you distinguish evidence for climate-driven extinction from evidence for human hunting pressure?

states.label: 2000 BC
states.summary: The last mammoths survived on Wrangel Island into the second millennium BC, while elephants still occupied a much wider geographic range than they do today.
states.interpretation: This state marks the transition from deep-time extinction into historical questions about shrinking elephant ranges and human societies.
states.question: How does the wider elephant range around 2000 BC complicate modern assumptions about where elephants 'belong'?

states.label: 1600 AD
states.summary: Expanding Atlantic commercial systems intensified extraction of ivory from parts of West Africa.
states.interpretation: The timeline now moves fully into historical systems of trade, labor, violence, consumption, and environmental pressure.
states.question: What evidence would be needed to connect growth in Atlantic commerce to changing elephant populations in West Africa?

states.summary: Zanzibar and East Africa became major centers in global ivory trading networks during the nineteenth century.
states.interpretation: This state connects elephant range contraction to commercial networks, material demand, transport systems, and imperial expansion.
states.question: How could historians connect ivory trade records to evidence of changing elephant populations in East Africa?
